ideas.title: Your Brain Burns Its Own Wiring Mid-Marathon
ideas.hook: During a marathon, the insulation on parts of your brain's wiring starts to thin out.
ideas.twist: Two months later it's all back, and scientists still can't say for sure why it happened.
visual: glowing brain whose nerve 'cables' dim as a fuel gauge empties
runner crossing mile 20 as the brain flickers
insulation slowly re-growing over a calendar
ideas.truth_note: Small 2025 Nature Metabolism study (10 runners): myelin dropped and recovered in ~2 months; 'used as fuel' is the authors' hypothesis.
ideas.code_shots: brain icon + fuel gauge emptying, calendar for the 2-month recovery (html beats: callout, gauge counter)
ideas.why: A scary-sounding but true-ish fact with an honest 'we don't fully know' twist keeps people to the end.

ideas.title: The Marathon Danger Hiding in Your Water Bottle
ideas.hook: At one Boston Marathon, about one in eight finishers had dangerously diluted blood from drinking too much.
ideas.twist: The runners in trouble weren't dehydrated: many actually finished heavier than they started.
visual: water bottles stacking up beside a runner
blood cells swelling as salt levels drop
scale at the finish showing the runner GAINED weight
ideas.truth_note: Almond et al., NEJM 2005: 13% of 488 sampled 2002 Boston finishers had hyponatremia; weight gain was a key risk factor.
ideas.code_shots: counter 13%, balance/scale at the finish, bottle icons (html: counter, compare)
ideas.why: Flips the 'drink more water' rule everyone believes, with a clean physical payoff on a scale.

ideas.title: Why Marathoners Hit a Wall at Mile Twenty
ideas.hook: Your body stores enough quick fuel for about twenty miles, and a marathon is twenty-six.
ideas.twist: Slow runners who burn more fat might never hit the wall at all.
visual: battery icon draining mile by mile
runner slamming into a literal wall at mile 20
slow runner jogging past the wall untouched
ideas.truth_note: Rough estimate: ~1,800–2,000 kcal of glycogen at ~100 kcal per mile empties around mile 18–20; varies with pace and body size.
ideas.code_shots: battery/fuel graph vs miles (html: graph, counter), runner icon
ideas.why: Every runner has heard of 'the wall'; seeing the math makes it click.

ideas.title: You Finish a Long Run Shorter
ideas.hook: You end a long run a few millimeters shorter than you started it.
ideas.twist: You grow it back overnight, and long-time runners actually have thicker spinal discs.
visual: spine discs squishing like sponges with each stride
ruler against the runner before and after
discs refilling while the runner sleeps
ideas.truth_note: Studies measure a few mm of height loss from disc compression during running; recovered with sleep; runners showed ~20% greater disc height.
ideas.code_shots: ruler + bone/disc callout, bed for overnight recovery
ideas.why: Weird, personal, measurable — viewers immediately want to check their own height.

ideas.title: Every Step Crushes Your Red Blood Cells
ideas.hook: Every footstrike of a long run destroys a few of your red blood cells.
ideas.twist: Cycling for the same hour destroys only about a quarter as many.
visual: foot slamming down on a capillary full of blood cells
cells popping with each step counter
same athlete on a bike, far fewer pops
ideas.truth_note: Telford et al. 2003: plasma free hemoglobin rose ~4x more after running than cycling at the same effort; small studies.
ideas.code_shots: bloodcell + footprint icons, compare beat running vs cycling
ideas.why: A hidden mechanical effect with a clear A-vs-B comparison twist.

ideas.title: Same Pace, Faster Heart: Cardiac Drift
ideas.hook: Run at exactly the same pace for two hours, and your heart beats faster anyway.
ideas.twist: Part of the fix isn't more training: it's staying cool and drinking enough.
visual: flat pace line next to a rising heart-rate line
blood volume shrinking as sweat drips
heart pumping harder to keep up
ideas.truth_note: Cardiovascular drift: heart rate rises during steady exercise from fluid loss and heat; reports of up to ~15%.
ideas.code_shots: graph with two lines (pace flat, HR rising), ecg + heart icons
ideas.why: Explains a number every watch-wearing runner has seen and wondered about.

ideas.title: How Much Water a Marathoner Sweats
ideas.hook: A marathoner can sweat out more than a liter of water every single hour.
ideas.twist: Elite winners often cross the line lighter by almost a tenth of their body weight, and still win.
visual: bucket filling under a running figure
liters counter climbing hour by hour
scale dropping at the finish
ideas.truth_note: Typical endurance-runner sweat rates ~1–1.5 L/h, range under 0.5 to over 2.5 L/h; one summary reports elite winners ~8.8% lighter at the finish.
ideas.why: Huge relatable quantities visualised as buckets of water.

ideas.title: The Runner's High Isn't Endorphins
ideas.hook: The famous runner's high probably isn't caused by endorphins.
ideas.twist: Runners given a drug that blocks endorphins still got high, and their cannabis-like chemicals rose instead.
visual: endorphin molecules blocked by a lock
runner still smiling past the block
a different molecule lighting up the brain
ideas.truth_note: 2021 study (63 runners, naloxone) found the high persisted; endocannabinoids rose; their full role is still debated.
ideas.why: Debunks a 'fact' everyone repeats, with a clever experiment as proof.

ideas.title: The First Marathon Story Is Probably Wrong
ideas.hook: The original marathon runner probably never ran from Marathon to Athens.
ideas.twist: The oldest account says he ran about two hundred forty kilometers to Sparta, and people still race that route today.
visual: map line Marathon to Athens fading out
a much longer line to Sparta drawing in
modern runners on the same ancient route
ideas.truth_note: Herodotus describes an Athens–Sparta run (~240 km); the Marathon–Athens run appears centuries later and is generally treated as legend.
ideas.code_shots: evidence-board/silent-film style; compare 42 km vs 240 km
ideas.why: A myth-busting history twist inside a running topic.

ideas.title: Marathons Make Your Blood Look Like a Heart Attack
ideas.hook: After a marathon, most runners' blood shows a marker doctors use to spot heart damage.
ideas.twist: Within a day it's back to normal, and in healthy runners it seems to be the heart simply working hard.
visual: blood test tube glowing red at the finish
ECG staying calm next to the alarming number
number dropping back overnight
ideas.truth_note: Transient cardiac troponin rises after marathons are well documented (e.g., 78% detectable at London; back to baseline within 24 h in a Belgian study).
ideas.code_shots: testtube + ecg + heart icons, counter for the marker, calendar/clock for 24 h
ideas.why: Alarming setup, reassuring and surprising payoff — strong retention arc.
